unit.title: Use workshop machines for basic operations

summary: This unit teaches you to use the basic machines of a fabrication workshop safely and accurately: the pedestal drill, the pedestal grinder, sawing machines, the centre lathe and the guillotine. You will learn the safety rules that apply to every machine, how to check, set up and use each one, how to choose speeds, how to handle cutting fluid and swarf, how to check your work against the drawing, and how to clean and care for the machines.

blocks.p: A welder spends much of the day away from the welding bay: cutting bar to length, drilling holes for bolts and hinges, grinding chamfers and sharpening tools, turning a pin, or shearing sheet. These jobs are done on **workshop machines**. Used well, they are quick and accurate. Used carelessly, they cause some of the worst injuries in any workshop, because a machine does not stop when it catches a sleeve, a glove or a finger.
**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other training centres, and anyone who uses the basic machines in a fabrication or maintenance shop.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Use only machines you are trained and allowed to use; dress correctly; check guards and the emergency stop; isolate before adjusting; never leave a machine running.
Prepare the machine and the work
Do the pre-start checks; mark out the work; hold it firmly; choose and fit the right drill, blade, wheel or tool; set the speed.
Drill, countersink and deburr holes in the right places on a pedestal drill.
Check and use a pedestal grinder to grind chamfers and sharpen tools.
Cut bar, tube and sections to length on a bandsaw, power hacksaw or abrasive cut-off saw.
Face, turn and centre drill simple parts on a centre lathe.
Cut sheet metal on a guillotine within its capacity.
Measure the finished part against the drawing and its tolerance; deburr it.
Switch off, isolate, clean the machine and area, look after cutting fluid and swarf, and report faults.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on machine safety, the drill, the grinder, sawing machines, the lathe, sheet metal machines, checking work, and cleaning and care.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as emergency stop, swarf, 118°, wheel dresser, countersink, three-jaw chuck, facing, tool rest, ring test, lockout, pilot hole, depth stop, reamer) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: marking out and drilling a hole pattern in a steel plate on the pedestal drill, with a countersunk hole; and cutting flat bar to length on a sawing machine and grinding chamfers on the pedestal grinder. The assessor watches your checks, dress, set-up and method as well as the finished parts.

blocks.note: Every machine has its own maker's instructions and the Centre has its own rules for it. This kit gives you the general method. Your instructor shows you the machines you will use, and you must not use one until you have been shown and given permission.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Use a machine only if you have been **trained** on it and given **permission** by your instructor or supervisor.
Read the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules for that machine.
Wear **safety glasses** (goggles or a face shield as well for grinding and abrasive cutting), **safety boots**, and ear protection where it is noisy.
**Remove rings, watches, bracelets and chains. Button or roll your sleeves, tuck in loose clothing, and tie back long hair.**
**Do not wear gloves near turning spindles, chucks, drills or blades.** A glove can be caught and pull your hand in before you can let go.

head: Check
Why
rows: Guards keep hands, clothing and flying chips away from moving parts
Emergency stop works and is easy to reach
To stop the machine at once if something goes wrong
No visible damage: cables, plugs, switches, belts, blades, wheels
Damaged parts can break, give a shock or start a fire
Chuck keys, spanners and loose tools removed
A key left in a chuck is thrown out at speed when the machine starts
Loose work can spin, fly out or break the tool
Area clear, dry and well lit
Slips and trips beside a running machine are very dangerous
No DO NOT USE tag on the machine
A tagged machine is faulty and must not be used

ul: Stay at the machine and give it your full attention. **Never leave a machine running** when you walk away: someone else could be hurt by it.
Keep your hands away from moving parts. Never reach over or around a running machine.
Do not talk to or distract someone using a machine. If you need them, wait until they have stopped.
Stop the machine fully before you measure, adjust, clean, or clear chips.
If a machine makes a strange noise, vibrates, smells hot or smokes: **stop it, isolate it, and report it**. Do not use it again until it has been checked.

blocks.p: The **emergency stop** is a large red, mushroom-shaped button. Pressing it stops the machine at once. It usually stays locked down until it is twisted or pulled out to reset. Know where it is on every machine before you start. In a group practical, one member stands by the emergency stop as a watcher while another works.
**Isolating** a machine means cutting it off from its power supply so that it cannot start. Pressing the stop button is **not** isolation: anyone could press start again.

ul: **When:** before opening covers to change belts or speeds; changing drills, blades or wheels; clearing a jam; cleaning inside guards; adjusting guards, blade guides or tool rests; and before any repair.
**How:** switch off at the machine, switch off at the isolating switch or unplug it, and wait until every moving part has stopped.

Where the Centre uses **lockout**, fit your own lock and a tag with your name and the date to the isolator, so nobody can switch it back on. Try the start button to prove the machine will not start, then return it to off.
Remove your lock and tag only when the work is finished and the guards are back in place.

blocks.note: Jamaica's mains supply is 110 V or 220 V at 50 Hz, and most workshop machines run on 220 V. Never open an electrical panel, change a plug or repair a cable yourself: only a qualified electrician does that. Report damaged cables and plugs.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Part
What it does
rows: The base stands on the floor (pedestal drill) or bench (bench drill); the column carries the table and head
Holds the work or the machine vice; it can be **raised, lowered and swung** round the column, and on many drills tilted
Drive the spindle; moving the belt between the stepped pulleys changes the speed. The belt cover must be closed when running
The spindle turns the drill; the quill carries it up and down
Lowers the drill into the work by hand
The chuck grips straight-shank drills; it is tightened with the key, which must be removed before starting
Holds taper-shank drills directly; they are removed with a drift
Stops the drill going deeper than a set amount, for blind holes and countersinks
Covers the chuck and drill while it turns

ul: **Shank:** the plain end held in the chuck (straight shank) or in the spindle (Morse taper shank).
**Body and flutes:** the spiral grooves carry the chips out and let cutting fluid in.
**Lips:** the two cutting edges at the point. The usual **point angle** for general work in steel is **118°**.
**Chisel edge:** the short edge across the centre of the point. It does not cut well; it pushes. This is why large drills need a pilot hole.
Drills are usually high-speed steel (HSS). Keep them sharp: a blunt drill squeals, overheats and makes rough, oversize holes.

blocks.p: Every material has a **cutting speed** that suits it: how fast the drill's outer edge should move over the metal, in metres per minute. The outer edge of a large drill travels further in each turn than a small one, so **large drills need a slower spindle speed, and small drills a faster one**. Hard materials need slower speeds than soft ones.

blocks.note: **N = (V × 1000) ÷ (π × D)**: N = spindle speed in rpm, V = cutting speed in m/min, D = drill diameter in mm, π ≈ 3.142.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Material (HSS drill)
Typical cutting speed
Fluid
rows: Cutting fluid or paraffin, to stop it sticking

head: Worked example: mild steel at 25 m/min
Working
Set (machine speeds 350, 600, 950, 1500, 2400 rpm)

blocks.p: Use the speed chart on the machine where there is one, and choose the nearest speed **below** the figure you work out. These figures are typical: follow the chart and your instructor.

head: Speed too fast
Speed too slow
rows: The drill overheats; its edges burn and go blunt, and may turn blue
Squealing; a rough or oversize hole
You push harder to make it cut, and small drills snap

blocks.note: To change speed on a belt-driven drill: switch off, **isolate**, and wait for the spindle to stop before you open the belt cover. Never hold a pulley to stop it, and never open the cover while it runs.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Never hold the work in your hand.** Clamp it in a **machine vice** or to the table with clamps.
If the drill grabs, unclamped work spins round like a blade. If that happens, hit the emergency stop and keep your hands away: never try to catch it.

When drilling right through, put **parallel packing** (or a block of scrap wood for sheet) under the work, or set it over the table's centre hole, so the drill breaks through into a gap and not into the vice or table.
Hold the vice against a stop or bolt it down for larger holes; the force on a large drill can turn a loose vice.

flow: Read the drawing; mark the hole centre with two crossing scribed lines, and **centre punch** it so the drill point does not wander
Do the pre-start checks; wear glasses, no gloves; secure sleeves, rings and hair
Clamp the work in the vice on packing; set the table height so the drill reaches with room to spare
Fit the pilot drill, tighten the chuck with the key, and **remove the key**
Set the speed for the pilot drill
Line the drill point up with the punch mark; drill the **pilot hole** with a steady feed and cutting fluid
Fit the final drill, set the slower speed, and drill to size
**Ease off the feed** as the drill breaks through the bottom
Stop the machine; deburr both sides of the hole; check its size and position
Brush the chips away with the drill stopped; clean the table

ul: A **pilot hole** is a small first hole drilled to guide a larger drill. It should be a little larger than the chisel edge of the big drill (often about 4–5 mm for a 10–12 mm drill), so the big drill cuts with its lips and needs less force.
For deep holes, lift the drill out every few millimetres to clear the chips ("pecking").
As the drill breaks through, it can grab the thin last layer of metal and pull itself in. Easing off stops it grabbing and breaking.

head: Operation
What it does
How
rows: A cone-shaped recess at the top of a hole so a countersunk screw sits flush (level with the surface)
Use a countersink bit at a slow speed; set the depth stop; check the depth with the screw and adjust a little at a time
A flat-bottomed step at the top of a hole for a cap screw head
Use a counterbore with a pilot that fits the hole
Finishes a drilled hole to an exact size with a smooth wall
Drill slightly undersize, then ream at a slow speed with fluid; never turn a reamer backwards
Holes that do not go right through

head: Fault
Likely causes
rows: No punch mark, no pilot hole, work moved, or the drill wandered on a curved or sloping surface
Blunt drill or unequal lips; speed too high; no fluid
Drill squeals, smokes, or chips come off blue
Speed too high, blunt drill, or no cutting fluid
Work not clamped, feeding too hard, chips jammed in the flutes, or grabbing at break-through

blocks.p: A **pedestal grinder** (or bench grinder) has a motor with a grinding wheel on each end, usually a coarse wheel and a fine one. It is used to grind chamfers, shape and sharpen tools such as chisels, centre punches and lathe tools, and remove burrs. Its wheels turn very fast: a cracked or misused wheel can burst and throw pieces with enough force to kill.

head: Part
What it does
rows: Abrasive grains held together by a bond; coarse for fast removal, fine for finishing
Cover the sides and most of the wheel; they hold the pieces if a wheel bursts
Supports the work close to the wheel
Clear screens over each wheel; you still wear safety glasses or goggles
The adjustable plate at the top of the guard opening

head: Check
Correct setting or condition
rows: No cracks or chips; face flat and not clogged or glazed
Right for the job: an ordinary aluminium oxide wheel for steel
**About 3 mm or less** between the rest and the wheel
Usually about 6 mm or less from the wheel
The wheel's maximum safe speed (printed on it) must be **at least** the grinder's speed (on its rating plate)

blocks.p: If the tool rest gap is too wide, the work can be dragged down into the gap between the rest and the wheel, jamming and cracking the wheel or pulling your fingers in. Adjust the rest only with the grinder **switched off and isolated**, and check the gap again whenever the wheel has been dressed or has worn smaller.

ul: Wheels are fitted only by a trained person, following the maker's instructions.
Check that the wheel's speed rating is at least the grinder's spindle speed. A wheel run faster than its rating can burst.

Do a **ring test** on the new wheel: hang it on a finger or a rod through the hole and tap it lightly with a non-metal tool (such as a screwdriver handle) on each side. A **clear ringing sound** means it is sound. A **dull thud** means it may be cracked: do not fit it.
Fit it with the right flanges and blotters (paper washers), and do not over-tighten the nut.

flow: Make sure you are allowed to use it; do the checks above; put on safety glasses or goggles; secure hair and clothing
**Stand to one side** as you switch on, and let the wheel run up to speed for a short time (about a minute for a new wheel). A damaged wheel is most likely to burst as it speeds up
Rest the work firmly on the tool rest and bring it gently to the **face** (the outside edge) of the wheel
Use light pressure and move the work across the face, so the wheel wears evenly
Dip the work in the water pot often to keep it cool
When you finish, switch off and let the wheel stop on its own; never slow it by pressing something against it

ul: **Never grind on the flat side of a straight wheel.** It is not made to take side pressure and can break.

**Never grind aluminium, brass, copper, lead or plastic on a steel-grinding wheel.** Soft metals clog (load) the wheel, which then overheats and can crack. Use a file or a wheel kept for those metals.
Never use a grinder with a missing guard or a cracked or chipped wheel. Tag it and report it.
Hold small parts in pliers or a holder, not between your fingertips.

blocks.p: To grind a 45° chamfer on the end of a bar, rest the bar on the tool rest and hold it firmly at 45° to the face of the wheel. Move it gently across the face with light pressure, turning it if you are chamfering all round, and cool it often in water. Check the chamfer with a rule or a 45° gauge.

Tools such as cold chisels, centre punches and lathe tools are hardened. If you grind them until the tip turns **blue**, the steel has overheated and **lost some of its hardness**, so the edge goes soft and blunts quickly. Grind lightly and cool often to keep the tip from changing colour. (Do not dip a hot carbide tool in water: the sudden cooling can crack it.)

A clogged, glazed or uneven wheel is trued up with a **wheel dresser** (a star dresser or a diamond dresser), which cuts away the worn surface to expose fresh, sharp grains and a flat face. Dressing is done by a trained person, with the tool rest used as a guide. After dressing, the wheel is smaller, so the tool rest gap must be reset (with the grinder isolated).

head: Machine
How it cuts
Good for
Safety points
rows: A continuous blade in a loop runs round two wheels, through guides, and feeds down through work held in a vice
Clean, straight cuts with little waste
Set the blade guide close to the work
Keep hands clear of the moving blade
The blade runs downwards through a table; the work is pushed into it by hand
Upper guide just above the work
Push small pieces with a push stick
A straight blade in a frame moves back and forth like a hand hacksaw; it cuts on one stroke only and lifts on the return
Bar and sections; simple and cheap to run
Keep clear of the moving frame
A thin abrasive disc spinning at high speed is pulled down through the work
Fast cuts in steel, including hard steel; angle and tube
Noisy, throws sparks, leaves a hot, burred edge
Sparks away from people and anything that burns
Face shield, goggles and ear protection

blocks.p: Blade teeth are counted in **teeth per inch (TPI)**. The rule is that at least **three teeth** should be in the metal at any time.

ul: **Thin material** (sheet, thin-wall tube): a **fine** pitch (many teeth per inch). With too few teeth in the cut, a tooth catches on the thin wall and strips off.
**Thick, solid bar:** a **coarse** pitch (fewer teeth), with room in each gullet for the chips.
Many shops fit a variable-pitch blade that covers a range of work. Follow the blade maker's chart.

Set the tension as the maker says, with the tension handle or gauge. A **loose blade** wanders, cuts crooked, can **slip off the wheels or snap**. A blade that is too tight strains the wheels and can break.

Set the **blade guide just above the work** (or just clear of it on a horizontal saw), as close as it will go. A guide left far from the work lets the blade twist, so the cut runs off square, and leaves more blade exposed.
Adjust guides and tension only with the saw **switched off and isolated**.
Check the blade for missing teeth, cracks and blunt teeth before you start.

blocks.h: Cutting bar to length on a horizontal bandsaw or power hacksaw

flow: Check the cutting list for the length and number of pieces
Check the saw: blade, tension, guides, guards, coolant level, vice; area clear
Wear safety glasses and boots; secure sleeves and hair
Mark the length, measuring from a **square end**, and allow for the width of the cut (the **kerf**, often 1–2 mm on a bandsaw)
Clamp the bar tightly in the vice with the mark lined up to the blade; support a long bar on a **roller stand** at the same height
Set the blade guide close to the work
Start the saw and let the blade come down **slowly and steadily** onto the work, without forcing it
When the saw has stopped, remove the piece: it may be hot and sharp
Deburr it and check its length and squareness; then cut the rest

ul: Work held loosely in the vice can move and snap the blade.
If the blade drops onto the work too fast, the teeth are broken or stripped. Set the feed (down-feed) control so the blade cuts steadily.
For many pieces of the same length, set the saw's **length stop** after checking the first piece, so every piece is cut the same.
Cut thin-wall tube and sections with the blade meeting as much metal as possible, and use a fine blade.
Check the disc for cracks and chips, and that its speed rating is at least the saw's speed. Fit discs only with the saw unplugged.
Clamp the work in the saw's vice. Never hold it by hand.
Set up a screen and make sure the sparks fly away from people, gas cylinders and anything that burns.
Wear a face shield over safety glasses, ear protection and gloves for handling the work.
Let the disc reach full speed before cutting; cut with steady pressure; never cut with the side of the disc.
Let the disc **stop fully** before you reach in to remove the cut piece. The cut end is hot and has a sharp burr.

blocks.p: On a **centre lathe** the **work turns** and a cutting tool is fed into it. It makes round parts such as pins, bushes, spacers and shafts.

head: Part
What it does
rows: The strong base, with accurate slideways (ways) along the top that the carriage and tailstock slide on
At the left: holds the motor drive, the gears or belts for changing speed, and the **spindle** that turns the work
Fitted to the spindle; grips the work in its jaws
At the right; slides along the bed. Holds a centre to support long work, or a drill chuck for drilling into the end of the work
Moves the tool along the bed
On the carriage; moves the tool in and out across the work
On the cross slide; can be set at an angle for short tapers and chamfers
Move the carriage by power, for turning and screw cutting
Chuck guard (often interlocked so the lathe will not start with it open), lead screw cover, emergency stop and foot brake

head: Chuck
Use
rows: All three jaws move together, so round (and hexagonal) bar is gripped centrally. Quick to use.
Each jaw moves on its own. Holds square, rectangular and odd-shaped work, and work that must be set off centre; can be set very accurately with a dial indicator.

blocks.note: **Never leave the chuck key in the chuck.** When the lathe starts, the key is thrown out at great speed. Make it a habit: your hand does not leave the key until the key is out of the chuck.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: The tip of the cutting tool must be **level with the centre height of the work**. Check it against the point of the tailstock centre, and pack it up with flat packing if it is low.
If the tool is **below** centre, it leaves a small **pip** in the middle when facing, and can dig in. If it is **above** centre, it rubs instead of cutting.
Keep the tool short in the tool post, and tighten it firmly.
Long work sticking out of the chuck more than about **three times its diameter** should be supported by the tailstock centre, or it bends and chatters (and can be thrown out).

head: Operation
What it does
rows: Makes the end of the bar flat and square to its length; the tool moves across the end
Makes the diameter smaller along the length; the tool moves along the bar
Makes a small, accurate cone-shaped hole in the end, to start a drill or take the tailstock centre
A drill in the tailstock is fed into the end of the turning work
Cuts an angled edge on the end of the bar
Cuts a finished part off the bar with a thin blade-like tool; slow speed, tool at centre height, cutting fluid
Presses a diamond or straight pattern into the surface for grip

blocks.p: The lathe uses the same formula as the drill, with D as the diameter of the **work**. At the same spindle speed, the surface of a large bar moves faster than a small one, so **large bars need a lower spindle speed**.

head: Worked example: mild steel, HSS tool, 25 m/min
Working
rows: 25 000 ÷ (3.142 × 40) ≈ 199 rpm: set the nearest speed below, about 190 rpm

ul: Turning steel can make long, stringy, blue-hot swarf that wraps round the work and the chuck. It is razor sharp.
Stop the lathe before you remove it, and pull it away with a **chip hook**, never your fingers or a rag.
To make the chips break up: use a tool with a **chip breaker** groove, or change the feed and depth of cut as your instructor shows you.

blocks.p: **Stop the lathe fully before measuring.** Never measure, file near, or wipe turning work: the jaws and work can catch your hand or the instrument.
A **guillotine** (shear) cuts sheet metal in a straight line with a long blade that comes down against a fixed blade. It may be worked by a foot treadle or by a motor.

head: Part
What it does
rows: The moving top blade shears the sheet against the fixed bottom blade
Press the sheet down just before the blade cuts, so it cannot move or lift
A guard in front of the blade and hold-downs that stops fingers reaching them
An adjustable stop behind the blade, for cutting many pieces the same width
A guide at 90° to the blade, for square cuts
Shows the thickest sheet the machine may cut (often less for stainless steel than for mild steel)

ul: Keep your **fingers behind the finger guard**, well away from the blade and the hold-down clamps.
**Never cut sheet thicker than the rated capacity**, and never cut rod, bar, wire or angle unless the machine is made for it. Overloading chips the blades and damages the machine.
Only one person works the guillotine. Make sure no one is behind it or near the treadle.
Keep your feet **off the treadle** while you place the sheet or adjust the gauges.
Sheared edges are sharp: wear gloves to handle the sheet (away from the blade), and deburr the edges.

head: Machine
Use
Safety
rows: Bends sheet along a straight line
Keep fingers out from under the clamping beam; watch the swinging bending leaf
Roll sheet into curves and cylinders
Keep fingers well away from the in-running rolls: they draw hands in
Cut notches and holes in sheet
Use the guards; keep fingers clear of the tool

sections.title: Cutting fluid, swarf and checking your work

blocks.p: Cutting fluid **cools** the drill, blade or tool and the work, so the edge does not overheat and go blunt. It **lubricates** the cut, so the tool cuts more easily and leaves a better finish, and it **washes chips** away from the cut.

ul: Use only the fluid the Centre supplies, mixed with water as the maker says (soluble oil is often mixed at about 1 part to 20, but follow the label).
Apply it with a brush, oil can or the machine's pump, never by hand near moving parts.
Cast iron and brass are usually machined dry.
Keep skin contact low; wash your hands after work and before eating; report any rash. Wear suitable gloves when handling containers of fluid, away from turning machines.
Wipe up spills at once so nobody slips.
Old fluid goes into the labelled waste container for proper disposal, **never down the drain or onto the ground**.

blocks.p: **Swarf** is the trade name for the chips, curls and dust cut off by a machine. It is sharp, and often hot.

ul: Never touch swarf with bare hands, and never blow it away with your mouth or with compressed air.
**Stop the machine**, then clear swarf with a brush or a chip hook.
Put it in the swarf or scrap bin, keeping different metals apart if the Centre recycles them.

blocks.p: Every part is measured and compared with the **drawing** before it is passed on. Do not guess by eye.

head: Check
Tool
rows: Steel rule, tape or vernier caliper
Squareness of cut ends and edges

blocks.p: The **tolerance** on the drawing says how much a size may vary. For example, 150 ± 0.5 mm allows any length from 149.5 mm to 150.5 mm. A part outside its tolerance is set aside and reported.

ul: Remove **burrs** (sharp, rough edges left by drilling, sawing and shearing) with a file or deburring tool, on both sides of holes and on all cut ends.
Mark finished parts as the job sheet asks (for example with your initials) and put them in the labelled place.

blocks.p: A clean, tidy machine is safer and gives better work. Chips and oil on the floor make people slip and cut themselves. Offcuts and tools left lying about are tripped over or fall into moving parts. Chips left on a drill table or lathe bed stop the work sitting flat, so holes and cuts come out wrong, and they score the slides. A tidy area also saves time: tools are easy to find.

blocks.h: At the end of a session

flow: Switch off and isolate the machine
Remove drills, keys, blades or cutting tools as the Centre's rules say, and put them back in their places
Brush the chips off the machine and table into the swarf bin (never with your hands, never blown at people)
Wipe off cutting fluid; oil bare steel surfaces as the Centre requires
Sweep the floor and wipe up spills
Put offcuts in the scrap bin and finished parts in their labelled place
Report any fault to your instructor or supervisor, and record it

ul: Never hose a machine down with water: it rusts the slides and gets into the electrics.
Oiling and greasing are done by a **trained person**, with the oil the **maker's chart** names, at the points and intervals it gives. The wrong oil, or none, wears out a machine.
Some shops release bandsaw blade tension at the end of the day; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.

head: Fault
What to do
rows: Missing or damaged guard; emergency stop not working
Do not use the machine. Isolate it, tag it DO NOT USE, report it
Cracked wheel, damaged blade or disc
Do not use it. Tag it and report it
Strange noise, vibration, burning smell, overheating
Stop and isolate the machine, report it
Isolate, tag and report; only an electrician repairs it
Clean up the spill and report it

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can follow the safety rules for every machine: training, dress, no gloves near turning parts, guards, emergency stop, never leaving a machine running.
I can explain isolation and lockout, and say when they are needed.
I can do the pre-start checks on a machine and report what I find.
I can name the parts of a pedestal drill and a twist drill.
I can work out a drilling speed and choose the right speed from the chart.
I can mark out, clamp, and drill a hole with a pilot hole, then countersink and deburr it.
I can check a pedestal grinder, set the tool rest gap, and grind a chamfer safely.
I can explain the ring test, wheel speed ratings and wheel dressing.
I can choose a sawing machine and blade, set the guide and tension, and cut bar to length allowing for the kerf.
I can use an abrasive cut-off saw safely.
I can name the main parts of a centre lathe, set a tool at centre height, and face and turn a bar.
I can use a guillotine safely within its capacity.
I can use cutting fluid and handle swarf safely.
I can measure finished parts against the drawing and its tolerance.
I can clean a machine and its area at the end of a session, and report faults.

terms: Chamfer
A small angled edge ground or cut on the corner or end of a part
Chip breaker
A groove or step on a lathe tool that breaks swarf into short pieces
Chisel edge
The short edge across the centre of a drill point; it pushes rather than cuts
Chuck key
The key that tightens a chuck; never left in the chuck
Countersink
A cone-shaped recess at the top of a hole for a flat-headed screw
Cutting speed
How fast the cutting edge moves over the metal, in m/min
Depth stop
A device on a drill that stops the drill going deeper than a set amount
Emergency stop
The red, mushroom-shaped button that stops a machine at once
Facing
Making the end of a bar flat and square on a lathe
Finger guard
The guard on a guillotine that keeps fingers away from the blade
Isolation
Cutting a machine off from its power so it cannot start
Kerf
The width of material removed by a saw cut
Lockout
Locking the isolator off, with a tag, while someone works on the machine
Pilot hole
A small first hole drilled to guide a larger drill
Point angle
The angle of a drill's point; 118° for general work
Reamer
A tool that finishes a drilled hole smooth and exactly to size
Ring test
Tapping a grinding wheel and listening for a clear ring to check it is not cracked
Swarf
Chips, curls and dust of metal cut off by a machine
Teeth per inch (TPI)
The number of teeth in each inch of a saw blade; its pitch
Three-jaw chuck
A self-centring lathe chuck whose jaws move together
Tool rest
The rest on a grinder that supports the work close to the wheel
Turning
Reducing the diameter of a bar along its length on a lathe
Wheel dresser
A tool that cleans and trues the face of a grinding wheel

c1.title: Shelf brackets on the pedestal drill in Lucea
c1.text: Jevaughn, a trainee at a training centre in Lucea, Hanover, must drill two 12 mm holes through each of eight brackets made from 8 mm mild steel flat bar. He has a 5 mm HSS drill for the pilot holes and a 12 mm HSS drill. The drill's speed chart offers 350, 600, 950, 1500 and 2400 rpm, and his instructor gives 25 m/min as the cutting speed for mild steel. The brackets are held in a machine vice on parallel packing.

c2.title: A new wheel for the grinder in Brown's Town
c2.text: Shantel works in the maintenance workshop of a school in Brown's Town, St Ann. The coarse wheel on the pedestal grinder is worn and is to be replaced by the trained technician. The grinder's rating plate gives 2,950 rpm. One new wheel in the store is marked "max 2,400 rpm"; another, marked "max 3,600 rpm", gives a dull thud when it is tapped. After the old wheel was dressed last week, the tool rest gap was left at about 9 mm. Later, Shantel sharpens a cold chisel on the fine wheel.

c3.title: Chair frames on the bandsaw in Junction
c3.text: Kadeem works at a furniture-frame shop in Junction, St Elizabeth. He must cut 25 × 25 × 1.5 mm square tube into 400 mm pieces on the horizontal bandsaw, from 6 m lengths, for a batch of chair frames. The saw has a coarse blade fitted for cutting solid bar, and its kerf is about 2 mm. The upper blade guide has been left at its widest setting from the last job.

c4.title: A hinge pin on the lathe in Port Maria
c4.text: Abigail is a trainee at a training centre in Port Maria, St Mary. She is making a hinge pin from 40 mm mild steel bar on the centre lathe, with the bar held in the three-jaw chuck and sticking out about 200 mm. When she faces the end, a small raised pip is left in the middle. As she turns the diameter, long blue strings of swarf curl round the work.

questions.q: Which speed should Jevaughn set for the 12 mm drill?
o: 350 rpm
600 rpm
950 rpm
1500 rpm
questions.why: N = (25 × 1000) ÷ (3.142 × 12) ≈ 663 rpm. The nearest chart speed below that is 600 rpm; 950 rpm would run the drill too fast and overheat it.

questions.q: Why does Jevaughn drill a 5 mm pilot hole before the 12 mm hole?
o: So the big drill needs less force and stays true
So the finished hole comes out a little over 12 mm
So the 12 mm drill can run at the pilot drill's speed
So no cutting fluid is needed for the larger drill
questions.why: The chisel edge at the centre of a large drill pushes rather than cuts. A pilot hole a little larger than that edge lets the 12 mm drill cut with its lips, needing less force and following the pilot.

questions.q: As the 12 mm drill breaks through, a bracket jerks loose from the vice and starts to spin. What should Jevaughn do?
o: Grab the bracket quickly to stop it spinning
Lift the drill out of the hole with the feed handle
Hit the emergency stop and keep his hands clear
Push the bracket against the column to stop it
questions.why: Spinning steel cuts like a blade, so hands stay away and the machine is stopped at once. Then he finds out why it came loose and eases off the feed at break-through next time.

questions.q: The 12 mm drill squeals and the chips come off blue. What is the most likely cause?
o: The vice is clamped too tightly on the bracket
The pilot hole was drilled too large
The feed is too light for a 12 mm drill
The speed is too high or the drill is blunt
questions.why: Blue chips and squealing mean too much heat at the cutting edges, from a speed that is too high, a blunt drill or no cutting fluid. He checks the speed, the drill and the fluid.

questions.q: Can the wheel marked "max 2,400 rpm" be fitted to this grinder?
o: Yes, as the two speeds are close enough
Yes, if the tool rest is set closer to it
No, it is rated for a lower speed than the grinder runs
No, it is rated for a higher speed than the grinder runs
questions.why: A wheel's maximum speed must be at least the grinder's speed. This grinder runs at 2,950 rpm, faster than the wheel's 2,400 rpm rating, so the wheel could burst.

questions.q: What does the dull thud from the 3,600 rpm wheel tell the technician?
o: The wheel may be cracked and must not be fitted
The wheel is a fine grade and gives a smooth finish
The wheel needs dressing before it is fitted
The wheel is damp and must dry before use
questions.why: In the ring test a sound wheel gives a clear ring, and a cracked one a dull thud. A cracked wheel can burst at speed, so it is not used.

questions.q: What should be done about the 9 mm tool rest gap?
o: Leave it, as a wider gap gives more room for large work
Close it up while the grinder is running so it can be seen
Pack the gap with a piece of steel to fill it
Isolate the grinder, then reset the rest to 3 mm
questions.why: A wide gap lets work be dragged down between the rest and the wheel, jamming or cracking the wheel and pulling fingers in. The rest is adjusted with the grinder isolated, and reset each time the wheel is dressed.

questions.q: The tip of Shantel's cold chisel turns blue as she grinds it. What has happened?
o: It got too hot and has lost some hardness
It has been ground to exactly the right angle
It has picked up oil from the grinding wheel
It has been hardened further by the grinding
questions.why: Blue shows the hardened steel got hot enough to soften, so the edge will blunt quickly. Light pressure and frequent cooling in the water pot keep the tip from changing colour.

questions.q: The coarse blade is fitted and the tube wall is only 1.5 mm. What should be done before Kadeem starts?
o: Turn the blade speed up to make the coarse teeth cut cleanly
Fit a finer blade so three or more teeth touch the wall
Fill the tube with sand so the coarse teeth have more to cut
Feed the blade down faster so each tooth cuts more metal
questions.why: At least three teeth should be in the metal at once. On a thin wall, coarse teeth straddle it, catch and strip, so a finer pitch is fitted, with the saw isolated.

questions.q: Allowing for a 2 mm kerf, how many 400 mm pieces can Kadeem cut from one 6 m length?
o: 13 pieces
14 pieces
15 pieces
16 pieces
questions.why: Each piece uses 400 + 2 = 402 mm of tube, and 6000 ÷ 402 = 14.9, so 14 whole pieces. Fifteen would need 6030 mm, more than the length (and the first end must be squared too).

questions.q: Kadeem's first cut comes out slanted, not square. Which is the most likely cause?
o: The blade speed is set too low for steel
The coolant has been mixed too weak
The blade guide is set far from the work
The down-feed is set too slow
questions.why: A guide far from the work lets the long free stretch of blade twist and wander, so the cut runs off square. The guide is set as close to the work as it will go, with the saw isolated.

questions.q: How can Kadeem make all the pieces the same length quickly?
o: Mark each piece from the end of the last offcut
Hold each piece against a tape measure while cutting
Cut them a little long and grind them all to length
Set the length stop, checked on the first piece
questions.why: A length stop, set and checked on the first piece, makes every piece the same without marking each one. Measuring from offcuts lets small errors build up.

questions.q: What causes the small pip left in the middle when Abigail faces the end?
o: The tool is below the centre height of the work
The tool is above the centre height of the work
The spindle speed is too low for the bar
The chuck jaws are gripping too tightly
questions.why: A tool set below centre cannot cut right to the middle and leaves a pip. She packs the tool up until its tip is level with the point of the tailstock centre.

questions.q: The bar sticks out about 200 mm from the chuck. What should Abigail do before turning its length?
o: Run the lathe faster so the bar stays straighter
Support the end with the tailstock centre
Take one deep cut so the job is over quickly
Grip only the very end of the bar in the chuck
questions.why: Work sticking out more than about three times its diameter bends away from the tool, chatters, and can be thrown out. Supporting the end with the tailstock centre keeps it rigid.

questions.q: With the lathe stopped, what can Abigail change to stop the long strings of swarf?
o: Turn off the chuck guard so the swarf can fly clear
Wrap the strings round the chuck to keep them tidy
Leave the strings until the end of the job
Use a tool with a chip breaker, or change the feed
questions.why: A chip breaker, or a change of feed and depth of cut, makes the swarf curl and break into short pieces. Long strings are razor sharp and are removed only with a chip hook when the lathe has stopped.

questions.q: Why might Abigail use a four-jaw chuck for her next job instead of the three-jaw?
o: The four-jaw grips round bar more quickly
The four-jaw needs no chuck key to tighten it
The job is square bar to be set off centre
The four-jaw lets the lathe run at a higher speed
questions.why: Each jaw of a four-jaw chuck moves on its own, so it holds square and odd-shaped work and can set work off centre. A three-jaw chuck is quicker for round bar.

questions.q: Javaun is setting the back gauge on a foot-operated guillotine. Where should his feet be?
o: Off the treadle and clear of it
Resting lightly on the treadle
On the treadle, ready to cut at once
Either way, as long as his hands are clear
questions.why: A foot resting on the treadle can bring the blade down while hands are near it. Keep your feet off the treadle until the sheet is placed, your hands are behind the guard, and you are ready to cut.

questions.q: After countersinking a hole, the screw head sits a little above the surface. What should you do?
o: Grind the top of the screw head flat with the plate
Cut a little deeper, trying the screw each time
Use a larger drill to open the hole right up
Hammer the screw in until its head is level
questions.why: Take a little more off with the countersink, using the depth stop, and try the screw each time. Cutting a little at a time stops you going too deep.

questions.q: A cutting list gives 150 ± 0.5 mm. Which piece must be set aside?
o: The piece at 149.6 mm
The piece at 150.0 mm
The piece at 150.4 mm
The piece at 149.4 mm
questions.why: The limits are 149.5 mm and 150.5 mm. The pieces at 149.6, 150.0 and 150.4 mm are within them; the one at 149.4 mm is too short.

questions.q: The coolant in a saw's tank has gone dirty and smelly and is to be changed. Where should the old fluid go?
o: Down the workshop drain with plenty of water
Onto the yard to keep the dust down
Into the labelled waste-fluid container
Back into the new drum to be used again
questions.why: Used cutting fluid pollutes drains, soil and water. It goes into the labelled waste container so it can be disposed of properly.
